The reliability and predictability of elaboration relies on several critical properties of the core type system, including decidability of judgemental equality and the injectivity of type constructors; these dependencies are witnessed in a concrete system by explicit calls to conversion checking and weak-head reduction subroutines.
  We introduce a dependently typed monadic domain specific language for the executable specification of correct-by-construction elaboration algorithms that is abstracted from any particular representation of normal forms or algorithm for conversion checking. In particular, we represent a bidirectionally typed surface language for Martin-Löf type theory by shallow embedding in this DSL so that the translation of surface terms into core terms amounts to elementary equational calculation. This translation is correct by construction in the sense that it cannot produce ill-typed terms, and is automatically stable under judgemental equality of core terms and even under substitution; from the latter property, we obtain a new denotational interpretation of the suspension of elaboration problems. Finally, a concrete elaboration algorithm is extracted by algebraic means from a presheaf model of the DSL built out of the bi-initial natural model of Martin-Löf type theory.
Programming Languages.comment: We have corrected a mistake in the formulation of η-conversion, and added several more proofs

Programming Languages.title: Contravariant Universe Subtyping, Formalized, Mechanized
Programming Languages.summary:
In a type theory with a cumulative universe hierarchy, \emph{subtyping} is often incorporated to lift lower universe levels to higher ones. In practice, kernels of proof assistants typically implement universe subtyping conservatively: subtyping only propagates covariantly into the output types of $Π$ types, while input types must be equivalent. A full-blown subtyping relation also compares the input types contravariantly. However, contravariant subtyping is not justified by the existing set-theoretic model, and poses challenges in the development of a complete subtyping algorithm.
  We present \mclttsub, a complete mechanized study of contravariant universe subtyping for a core Martin-Löf type theory (MLTT), built as an extension of the verified McTT kernel in Rocq. We re-establish the syntactic meta-theory and the soundness and completeness properties of the normalization-by-evaluation (NbE) algorithm. To complete the verified pipeline for a type-checker, we give two complete and sound subtyping algorithms. The first one \emph{renormalizes} output types in every $Π$ iteration. Despite a simple completeness proof, this algorithm incurs additional computational cost. The second algorithm hence circumvents this cost by avoiding the renormalization at all. It simply recursively compares two already normalized types structurally. Nevertheless, a completeness proof of this algorithm in a semantic approach requires to reason about normalization in sub-contexts, a capability beyond what the current semantic gadget offers. Instead, we conduct a program equivalence proof through bisimulation relations. Using this technique, we prove that the NbE algorithm returns equal normal forms in sub-contexts up to universe levels, and successfully conclude the completeness of the subtyping algorithm.

Programming Languages.title: Mechanising Denotational Semantics in Agda
Programming Languages.summary:
Mechanisation of a mathematical definition (also referred to as formalisation) has many benefits. Here, we focus on mechanising denotational semantic definitions of programming languages by embedding them in the Agda language. The Agda type-checker detects and reports any issues with the wellformedness and type correctness of the embedded definitions.
  To minimise the effort required, and to facilitate correlation of the original definition with its Agda embedding, mechanisation should not involve significant reformulation or extension. Here, we show how to embed conventional Scott-Strachey denotational definitions in Agda with almost no changes to $λ$-notation or domain equations.
  Agda notation for definitions of types and functions corresponds closely to the conventional meta-notation of denotational semantics. We have developed a collection of Agda modules with postulated types for commonly used domain constructors and their associated operations.
  We illustrate our approach with mechanisations of three denotational definitions: a model of the untyped $λ$-calculus, Plotkin's denotational semantics of PCF, and a semantics of a sublanguage of Scheme. In previous work, similar mechanisations in Agda have revealed several unsuspected wellformedness issues in published denotational definitions.
  Some of the postulated properties of our definitions are inconsistent with a classical set-theoretic interpretation of Agda. We conjecture that they would be consistent with an interpretation of Agda in a higher-order intuititionistic logic, such as that used by Simpson in his work on synthetic domain theory. After recalling previous work on mechanising domain theory, we consider the possibility of mechanising synthetic domain theory in Agda.
Programming Languages.comment: 23 pages, excl. references. To be published in Proceedings of MFPS 2026

Programming Languages.title: (Implicitly) Characterizing Probabilistic Polynomial Time as Used in Cryptography
Programming Languages.summary: In this paper, we show how a recently introduced $λ$-calculus for randomized computation, called $λ\mathbf{BLL}$, can accurately capture the notions of first- and second-order polytime computations used in cryptographic definitions and proofs. These results, spelled out in the style of so-called \emph{implicit computational complexity}, imply that $λ\mathbf{BLL}$ is sufficiently powerful to express experiments and adversaries as used in cryptography, and that reductions, when formulated within the calculus, are guaranteed to be complexity-preserving. Remarkably, while polynomial-time soundness holds for the full calculus, polynomial-time completeness already follows in presence of a minimal finite set of basic functions.
Programming Languages.comment: Extended version of a paper to appear in the proceedings of FSTTCS 2026

Programming Languages.title: sGLP: Specifying Stochastic Agents that Simulate People
Programming Languages.summary:
Grassroots platforms are designed to be owned, operated and governed by their participants, and thus are constituted from person-to-person smartphone apps that run on participants' smartphones. A grassroots app is specified using a grassroots social contract, which is compiled through an abstraction cascade into a volition-guarded Grassroots Logic Program (vGLP), a multiagent concurrent logic programming language. A vGLP program in turn specifies a smartphone UI via which people express their volitions and thus control the app. Prudence dictates large-scale evaluation and testing of grassroots platforms prior to deployment, but using the many people needed to do that is a contradiction in terms. Hence another solution is needed.
  Here, we present stochastic GLP (sGLP), designed to allow grassroots platforms to be simulated at scale from the vGLP programs that deploy them, with stochastic agents in place of people. sGLP is GLP with a rate extension for specifying stochastic behaviour. A stochastic agent is an sGLP program replacing both the vGLP UI and the person behind it. It is typed by the dual of the interactive type of the UI and specifies a stochastic profile of a person's behaviour.
  We demonstrate sGLP on the grassroots social graph, with a population of men and women drawn from four stochastic profiles --- homophile or indifferent, wary or sociable --- and on grassroots currencies, with four profiles --- spenders or savers, cautious or generous --- and report what the mix of profiles does to the social graph that forms and to the currencies that circulate.
  We prove that every run of a vGLP program in which sGLP agents replace the UI and the people behind it is a vGLP run. We implemented sGLP in GLP by Gillespie's method, and ran reproducible simulations with it.

Programming Languages.title: Kaizen: Metamorphic Fuzzing and Differential Testing for LLM-Translated HPC Applications
Programming Languages.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to port scientific codes across heterogeneous high-performance computing (HPC) programming models, such as translating CUDA to OpenMP, OpenACC, Kokkos or SYCL. However, current evaluations use compilation success, token-level similarity, or developer-written tests from static benchmarks, which cannot reliably ensure behavioral correctness. We present Kaizen, a metamorphic fuzzing and differential testing framework for evaluating the correctness of LLM-translated HPC code. Kaizen uses metamorphic fuzzing via source-code mutation to generate semantically equivalent programs, grammar-based input fuzzing to explore behavioral diversity, and differential testing to expose semantic divergences between original and translated applications that compile and pass developer-written tests yet produce incorrect scientific results. We evaluate Kaizen on CUDA-to-OpenMP translation of 16 scientific applications from seven domains using three fine-tuned LLMs at kernel-level and full-program granularity. Our evaluation reveals that (1) compilation success is a poor proxy for correctness; (2) LLM-translated programs exhibit systematic compile-time error patterns, with nine categories for kernel-level translation and 27 for full-program translation; (3) semantic errors that survive compilation are often input-dependent and require differential testing to expose; and (4) full-program translation is substantially harder than kernel-level translation. These findings highlight the need for correctness-oriented evaluation of LLM-assisted HPC code translations.
Programming Languages.comment: 28 pages

Software Engineering.title: Rethinking Software Development as a Self-Adaptive Socio-Technical System
Software Engineering.summary: Agentic AI is substantially shortening the timescale at which development context (e.g., goals, evidence, uncertainty, and risk) evolves. However, human-agent organization across development tasks is typically treated as fixed, which is problematic because development configurations may become suboptimal as the development context changes. We propose viewing software development as a self-adaptive socio-technical system in which both the software project and the development configuration (participants, responsibilities, authority, information, and verification) adapt as the development context evolves. This yields two coupled forms of adaptation: evolving the software and reconfiguring how subsequent engineering is performed. We illustrate the idea with a proof of concept, outlining challenges and future plans.

Software Engineering.title: When the Approved File Is Unchanged: Authority-Set Integrity for Deployment and Coding-Agent Approvals
Software Engineering.summary: An approval for a deployment, a release, or an agent-issued command is recorded against one object: a workflow file, a script, a command line. The run that follows also reads other repository files, which decide what the deployment creates and which changes a policy allows, so an edit to one of them after approval passes any check on the approved object. Such edits are the common case. In the history of 20 public repositories, 296 of the 542 commits that change a file the run reads (54.6%) leave the approved file untouched, all of them ordinary development with no adversary involved. We demonstrate the consequence on two of those repositories: an edit outside the approved workflow adds a bucket-write policy to a deployed role, a one-line edit removes the human approval required for high-risk changes, and a check on the approved file accepts both. We define authority-set integrity: an approval is sound when it binds every repository file the authorized run is configured to read, and exact when it binds no other file. A binding over that set rejects both edits and re-requests a standing approval on about one commit in ten. The hard part is naming the set. Coding agents asked to produce the binding compute the digest correctly and bind different file sets from run to run, so a checker cannot take the set on the agent's word. It should compute the digest itself and draw the set from a source it can verify, such as the deployment tool's own record of its inputs or a manifest declared in the repository.

Software Engineering.title: TurnCost: Turns, Not Observations: Cache-Aware Loop Engineering for Coding Agents
Software Engineering.summary:
AI coding agents operate in iterative loops: they modify code, run tools, inspect the results, and decide what to do next. We call the design of this process loop engineering, which includes context management, model selection, compaction, and termination. Existing efficiency work mainly compresses tool observations or routes selected turns to cheaper models, but the practical opportunity for these optimizations remains unclear. We analyze 600 publicly released coding-agent trajectories spanning two agent scaffolds and two language models. Median observations contain only 118-286 tokens, while the large build logs commonly used to motivate compression occur near the ninety-ninth percentile. Moreover, 98.6% of input tokens are served from a prefix cache, so flat input pricing overestimates loop cost by roughly 7x on average under near-ideal caching.
  We derive and empirically validate a closed-form break-even condition for model delegation. Delegation increases cost in half of the evaluated settings, near the predicted boundary. More broadly, turn count explains 84% of the variance in log trajectory cost, compared with 4% for mean observation size; the most expensive trajectories have the most turns despite having the smallest observations. These associations suggest that observation-focused methods target a secondary cost factor, and identify unnecessary turns as the larger and largely unexamined opportunity, though we do not establish that turns can be removed while holding task success fixed. We release TurnCost, a tool for re-scoring trajectory corpora under alternative caching, pricing, compression, and routing policies.

Software Engineering.title: Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today's and Future AI Agent Systems
Software Engineering.summary: Claude Code is an agentic coding tool that can run shell commands, edit files, and call external services on behalf of the user. This study describes its architecture by analyzing the publicly available source code and comparing it with two independent open-source AI agent systems, OpenClaw and Hermes Agent, that answer many of similar or even the same design questions. Our analysis identifies five human values, philosophies, and needs that motivate the architecture: human decision authority, safety, security, and privacy, reliable execution, capability amplification, and contextual adaptability. We then trace them through thirteen design principles to implementation choices. The core of the system is a simple while-loop that calls the model, runs tools, and repeats. Most of the code, however, lives in the systems around this loop: a permission system with seven modes and an ML-based classifier, a five-layer compaction pipeline for context management, four extensibility mechanisms (MCP, plugins, skills, and hooks), a subagent delegation and orchestration mechanism, and append-oriented session storage. Comparisons with OpenClaw and Hermes Agent show that the same design questions produce different answers across three deployment contexts. Claude Code emphasizes per-action safety, OpenClaw emphasizes perimeter-level access, and Hermes renders per-action approvals across many surfaces. At the runtime layer, Claude Code uses a single CLI loop, OpenClaw embeds the runtime within a gateway control plane, and Hermes uses one process whose role is set by its entry point. At the context and extension layer, Claude Code extends the context window, OpenClaw registers gateway-wide capabilities, and Hermes provides pluggable memory and model backends. We finally identify six open design directions for future agent systems, grounded in recent empirical, architectural, and policy literature.

Software Engineering.title: Humans vs. Machines: A Comparison With AI Agents in Software Reverse Engineering
Software Engineering.summary: Can an autonomous AI agent reverse engineer a binary as well as a skilled human analyst? Do they adopt the same strategy, and can agents scale to real-world programs? We compare human and LLM-based software reverse engineering (SRE): nine models tackle two compact static-analysis challenges previously solved by human analysts, scored with a common understanding rubric, and we record their complete interactions with IDA Pro. This lets us compare not only what humans and agents recover, but also how they investigate a binary. The best agents (GPT-5.5 Pro, Claude Opus 4.8, and Kimi K3) achieve statistically human-competitive understanding on both tasks, while weaker models remain far behind. Ablations show that the gap depends on code representation and workflow demands, not on model capability alone: open-weight models improve substantially with richer code representations, whereas frontier models show no significant change. Similar success rates hide different workflows. Humans repeatedly revisit functions and follow local program structure; strong agents jump across the binary, retrieve information broadly, and rarely return to inspected code, a behavior we call greedy fetching. This strategy is not fixed: given semantically richer code, agents fetch less without losing understanding. Because greedy fetching aggregates large amounts of code in the agent's context, we measure context-window saturation across 4,000 real-world binaries: large windows accommodate many programs, but larger applications and lower-level representations quickly exhaust them. Autonomous reverse engineering is becoming competitive, with a large speed advantage, but scaling it will require better navigation, selective retrieval, and persistent analysis state, not merely larger context windows.

Software Engineering.title: AI-Native Product Management: A Vision
Software Engineering.summary: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to support product management tasks. At the same time, AI-native research and development (R&D) may increase software realization capacity. Organizations may realize software faster than they can identify, qualify, and reconsider what should be realized. This paper asks how product management should be re-envisioned under these conditions. We synthesize research on software product management, product learning, human-AI collaboration, and the Product Management and R&D boundary. We propose a vision in which AI becomes a persistent participant in product work. The vision covers sensing, exploration, decision-making, realization, and learning. We propose six principles and make the vision tangible through an operating model grounded in human professionals, AI personas, agents, skills, and a shared product context. We further argue that AI-native Product Management and AI-native R&D can form a continuous product-learning process. Finally, we identify four AI-specific research directions that require empirical investigation.

Software Engineering.title: Testuary: Agentic Test Generation with Zero-Shot Parallelism
Software Engineering.summary: Agentic approaches for automated test generation can reach high-quality results, but they improve a given test suite incrementally, so a weak starting point may lead to many iterations or insufficient tests. To address this, we present Testuary, which provides the agentic phases with an improved starting point. Testuary first generates multiple test suites through independent, parallel zero-shot requests, checks and repairs them deterministically, and combines them into a single suite with a novel structural merging approach. A runtime-weighted set-cover reduction removes redundant tests without losing covered lines, branches, or killed mutants. After that, two agentic phases target the remaining gaps in coverage and mutation score. We compare Testuary with established search and LLM-based test generation approaches. The non-agentic first phase alone already significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art. After the agentic phases, Testuary achieves on average more than 99.9% line and branch coverage as well as a mutation score of 98.6%, significantly outperforming all compared baseline approaches. Testuary needs fewer model requests and its test suites are on average smaller and faster than those of the compared agentic approach.

Software Engineering.title: Do Modifications Made by Coding Agents Make Subsequent Software Maintenance Harder?
Software Engineering.summary: Coding agents increasingly maintain repositories over time, where each change becomes the starting point for subsequent tasks. Yet existing benchmarks either start tasks from developer-written code or cannot separate later-task difficulty from the effects of an agent's earlier changes. We ask whether agent-written code makes subsequent maintenance harder and whether the cost stems from inherited test failures or the code itself. We introduce SWE-Maintain, comprising 100 three-event maintenance episodes from 50 real-world Python repositories, with hidden tests certified across each sequence. Each later task is evaluated twice with the same agent and tests: from the developers' preceding patches (Developer-History) and from the agent's own changes (Agent-History). Across five coding systems, two backbone models, and 1,996 paired later events, Agent-History reduces later-task resolution by 5.6 percentage points on average. When success additionally requires all earlier tests to pass, the gap reaches 14.0 points. Two-thirds of Agent-History starting repositories already fail earlier tests, and only 1.9% of events starting from those states end with all accumulated tests passing. When the inherited code passes earlier tests and the next task is not already solved, the disadvantage disappears (+2.7 points; 95% CI [-0.5, +6.1]). These findings suggest that the main downstream cost of agent-written changes lies in inherited test failures rather than a measurable maintenance disadvantage in code that preserves earlier tested behavior. Evaluations should therefore include agent-produced history, and coding agents should preserve earlier behavior across changes.

Software Engineering.title: FlowArk: Boosting Agentic Data-flow Analysis for Android Apps via Context-Aware Knowledge Reuse
Software Engineering.summary:
Data-flow analysis is foundational to Android app privacy and security auditing. Recent coding agents can assist with non-trivial source-to-sink data-flow analysis tasks by searching, reading, and reasoning over repository code. However, when these tasks are executed as a batch workload, current agentic analysis setups incur substantial re-analysis cost. Agent instances assigned to different taint sources may inspect shared code fragments, because code reuse in the target app can cause different data-flow paths to converge on shared program logic. Since these agent instances are context-isolated, analysis of these shared code fragments can be repeated within a batch, unnecessarily consuming API budget and limiting scalability.
  We propose FlowArk, a knowledge-reuse system that reduces re-analysis cost in batch agentic data-flow analysis by making knowledge from completed analyses available to later agent instances. Specifically, FlowArk distills completed analysis histories into reusable knowledge candidates, packages these candidates into matchable knowledge entries, and injects matched entries into a later agent instance's context. We implement FlowArk on OpenCode and evaluate it on 4,649 source-to-sink data-flow analysis tasks from 49 open-source Android apps. Compared with standard OpenCode, FlowArk-enabled OpenCode maintains comparable analysis quality while reducing end-to-end API cost by 26.91%. This cost-reduction trend holds across different LLM backends and repeated runs.

Software Engineering.title: TileCas: Cascading Kernel Development Across Programming Abstractions
Software Engineering.summary: Programming abstractions have traditionally been designed for humans, but code generation is increasingly performed by models and autonomous agents. We investigate abstractions for machine-driven programming through GPU and AI-accelerator kernel generation. High-level domain-specific languages (DSLs) simplify search by delegating implementation details to compilers, while lower-level representations provide finer-grained control at the cost of a larger and more complex search space. In this paper, we present TileCas, a unified, pluggable interface that enables coding agents to develop kernels across multiple editable abstraction levels. Rather than committing to a single representation, TileCas allows an agent to transfer and refine candidates across levels through Cross-Level Diagnosis, which maps correctness and performance feedback to actionable controls at different abstraction levels; Abstraction Scheduling, which selects both the candidate and representation from which subsequent refinement should proceed; and a Heterogeneous Search Tree, which preserves and revisits alternative search trajectories spanning multiple representations. We integrate TileCas with two code agents AKO and KDA, and evaluate both integrations on 50 end-to-end KernelBench Level 3 workloads across two accelerator platforms and two language models. Giving equal weight to the four accelerator-model configurations, AKO with TileCas achieves an arithmetic-mean speedup of $4.84\times$, compared with $3.75\times$ for the strongest evaluated baseline without TileCas, an improvement of 29.0%. Integrating the same interface with KDA improves its mean speedup by 69.2%, with gains in every configuration. These results show that allowing coding agents to navigate across programming abstractions can improve machine-driven software development and can be reused across different base workflows.

Software Engineering.title: Does Failure Feedback Direct Agent Self-Modification?
Software Engineering.summary: Self-improving agents use failure feedback to revise their code or instructions, but gains after selection do not establish target-specific repair or generalization. We measure directedness by comparing repair of a randomly selected target failure with repair of the parent's other failures. Across 145 eligible modifications in public Darwin Gödel Machine logs, we find no detectable target-specific advantage. Controlled instruction-revision experiments with small open models show that relevant feedback can improve target repair. In a second study with a pre-specified analysis plan, target feedback raised repair by 20 percentage points for Qwen3-4B relative to matched same-category feedback; the 7-point increase for Phi-4-mini was not significant. Target repair did not reliably imply held-out improvement. Held-out gains were concentrated in settings with identifiable, repairable failure mechanisms, including planted errors and natural tool-interface failures. Benefits of edit localization and regression screening varied across settings, while eight-step revision loops and GEPA ended at similar mean held-out accuracy. Evaluations should report target repair, transfer to related failures, and held-out net change separately.
Software Engineering.comment: 28 pages, 8 figures, 8 tables. Code, derived data and a script that rederives every number in the paper are included as ancillary files

Software Engineering.title: Executable but Unfaithful: Mock Object, Stub, and Assertion Generation by LLMs and Coding Agents
Software Engineering.summary:
Mocking is a foundational practice in unit testing, enabling developers to isolate the code under test by replacing real dependencies with simulated alternatives. Automating the generation of mock objects, stubs, and mock assertions has been a long-standing research goal. However, capture-and-replay approaches rely on recording the runtime behavior of actual dependencies. Evolutionary approaches such as StubCoder overcome this requirement but constrain generation to predefined symbol pools. Large language models (LLMs) and coding agents offer an alternative by generating mocking artifacts from source code without requiring recorded dependency executions or fixed symbol pools. Yet, no systematic study has evaluated their capabilities across all three artifact types.
  To address this gap, we construct MockBench, a benchmark comprising 165 mock artifact generation tasks from real-world Java and Python projects, with validated reference mock objects, stubs, and mock assertions. We evaluate six LLMs and three coding agents in terms of executability, behavior fidelity, and interaction-fault detection capability, complemented by comparisons with existing tools and sensitivity analysis. Experimental results show that LLMs and coding agents indeed have been the state-of-the-art techniques in mock-based testing. More specifically, compared with LLMs, coding agents substantially improve executability, while these gains do not consistently translate into higher behavior fidelity or better interaction-fault detection. Furthermore, we analyze 660 failures from LLMs and coding agents, and identify ten error types across the three artifact categories, revealing behavioral deviations that passing tests can conceal. Our findings highlight the challenges of mock artifact generation and provide practical guidance for both developers and researchers.

Software Engineering.title: How Much Can Repeated Running Buy? A Measured Variance Ceiling for LLM Code Evaluation
Software Engineering.summary: A benchmark score is a measurement whose uncertainty has two sources: an aleatoric component from stochastic decoding and an epistemic component from the finite problem set. Using 16 models on 99 recent LeetCode-style problems with two prompts and five runs each (15,840 judged runs in a fully crossed design), we estimate both components and ask a design question: how much can repeated running buy? First, the pooled-binomial interval that repeated-run protocols invite answers neither question of interest---it is about $2\times$ too narrow for generalisation to new problems and $2\times$ too wide for the fixed problem set---and under correctly clustered intervals, 12 of 15 adjacent leaderboard pairs are statistically unresolved. Second, the variance ceiling $1+μ_w/σ_b^2$, the largest factor by which repetition can reduce score variance, has median 1.34 across models (range 1.05--1.71), so repetition can narrow confidence intervals by at most 23% on this benchmark, and by 14% for the median model. Third, once the cost of adding verified problems is priced in, the precision-optimal repeat count is $R^{*}=\sqrt{μ_w c_p/(σ_b^2 c_g)}$, and the variance curve is flat around it: on this benchmark the decisive reason to repeat is not precision but identification---two to three runs suffice to estimate the components that the ceiling and the fixed-benchmark interval require. All three are measurements of one benchmark at one decoding temperature, and we state explicitly what they do and do not license.
Software Engineering.comment: 17 pages, 4 figures, 11 tables. Substantially revised and retitled from v1; reframes the original repeated-run evaluation data as a variance decomposition, with expanded statistical validation and experimental details. Data and code: https://github.com/Yongxi-Zhou/leetcode-evaluator-data-output . Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AI for Verifiable Coding (VeriCodeGen)

Software Engineering.title: Verification as an Architectural Layer for LLM Agents: A V-Model Design, and a Pilot Study of Its Deterministic Core
Software Engineering.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents built on the ReAct pattern concentrate four responsibilities in one model: selecting a strategy, choosing each action, formatting it, and judging whether the result is adequate. Nothing outside the generative loop can reject its output, so an agent that cannot make progress does not report failure; it runs until an external budget stops it. We propose treating verification as an architectural layer by adapting the V-model from software engineering: specification levels descend from requirements to individual steps, each level is paired with a dedicated verifier, a deterministic controller enforces every verdict, and only verification outcomes write to memory, so a rejection localizes the level that introduced the fault and an agent halts by declining rather than by exhaustion. Each verifier separates a zero-cost deterministic \emph{gate} from an optional LLM \emph{judge}, so the contribution and cost of each can be measured independently. We report a pilot implementing the acceptance- and unit-level verifier pairs, comparing five configurations that share one executor, tool set, and scorer and differ only in verification, on the four-hop stratum of MuSiQue with an 8B-parameter backbone. Across 47 executions, the two unverified configurations answered none of ten questions, every run ending at a step cap or provider token limit; the verified configuration without a planner answered eight and abstained on the rest. Deterministic gates produced eight of the nine observed corrections at zero marginal cost, and planning degraded performance once verification was present. These results characterize termination behavior, not accuracy at scale; we outline a twelve-month plan to complete and evaluate the full architecture, including the integration-level pair the pilot omits.

Software Engineering.title: LASER: Defeasible Certificate Search for Long-Range Protocol Dependencies
Software Engineering.summary: Protocol specifications rarely justify executable behavior in one place: a transition may inherit its source state from a remote control block, name its events only by number, and remain subject to a later correction. Recovering the nearby clause is therefore insufficient; the system must assemble a source-linked certificate and determine whether any stronger rule applies. We introduce LASER, a proof-carrying search method for sparse, defeasible protocol evidence. LASER represents missing support and unresolved corrections as explicit obligations, searches typed evidence routes, and lets an occurrence-aware symbolic checker alone decide whether a certificate warrants, refutes, or leaves a behavior unresolved. On 91 BehaviorCheck families under a matched 2K budget, LASER improves Joint Edge+Proof over the strongest local reader on two model families ($Δ=+.132$, $p=.017$; $Δ=+.198$, $p<.001$) while cutting false discoveries by 2--3$\times$. Controlled replays attribute the gain and its limits: neither reference routing nor deterministic citation expansion alone exceeds the local baseline; whole-document reading (29--65K tokens), two-round iterative retrieval, and even oracle minimal-certificate evidence all fail to reach LASER, localizing the bottleneck in typed obligation closure rather than evidence access. An authority-corruption replay shows source-link errors only cause abstention, while the only unsafe-warrant mechanism is mis-recording a Held erratum as Verified, confined to that erratum's family. LASER thus improves long-range dependency recovery while converting incomplete evidence and uncertain authority into explicit residual obligations rather than unsupported behavior.

Software Engineering.title: Bulkhead: Automated Semantic Detection and Remediation of Container Escape Vulnerabilities
Software Engineering.summary:
Container filesystem isolation depends on safely resolving container-controlled paths during privileged host-container interactions. As third-party plugins and agent sandboxes introduce more interactions, unsafe path resolution can redirect host operations across isolation boundaries, expanding the attack surface for path traversal vulnerabilities. These logic flaws are difficult to mitigate: kernel defenses require intrusive redesign, static rules miss cross-boundary semantics, and manual auditing cannot scale. Large Language Model (LLM) based methods can detect syntax flaws through stable code patterns and identify logic flaws in domains such as smart contracts by comparing equivalent implementations. Container components, however, provide neither form of regularity: their heterogeneous interfaces operate under trust boundaries, filesystem views and interaction orders, making the security invariant difficult to find.
  We present Bulkhead, an automated framework for detection and remediation. Bulkhead summarizes historical CVEs into structured semantic patterns, correlates documentation with entry and effect side code evidence, and recovers source-to-sink execution contexts. Grounded patterns guide LLM reasoning, while isolated Proof-of-Concept (PoC) execution validates findings. For remediation, Bulkhead generates repository-specific patches, checks that they build, and iteratively verifies path safety and functionality using pattern derived model checking templates and counterexamples before runtime validation. Across container repositories, Bulkhead discovered 20 zero-day vulnerabilities, accounting for 43% of the total number discovered over the past decade. Among them, 3 have been assigned CVEs and the verified patch suggestions have been submitted to the upstream.

Software Engineering.title: HarnessSecurity-Bench: Do Security Mechanisms Really Protect Coding Agent Harnesses?
Software Engineering.summary: Coding agent harnesses mediate tool use and authorize actions, yet their security mechanisms and runtime effects remain incompletely characterized. We present HarnessSecurity, the first systematic empirical study and benchmark of open- and closed-source coding agent harnesses. First, we derive a ten-mechanism taxonomy and then assess 400 harness-mechanism cells using independent ratings by researchers and large language model (LLM) judges. We find that about half of confirmed mechanism implementations are opt-in, while closed-source harnesses exhibit substantial evidence gaps. Second, we introduce HarnessSecurity-Bench, a benchmark of 23 tasks across five attack surfaces without sacrificing legitimate task requirements. Using separate deterministic oracles to measure task utility and attack effects with security setting comparisons, we evaluate nine mechanisms across six leading harnesses: Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, gptme, Qwen Code, and GitHub Copilot. Under a controlled LLM baseline GLM-5.2, we conduct 2,500 trials, recording 81,155 tool calls and over 2.2 billion tokens. Enabling auto-approve increases utility and raises attack success from 29.2% to 95.6%. Network isolation and read-only mode reduce attack effects with substantial utility losses, while command allowlisting and command denylisting reduce attack effects with a small utility loss and a utility gain, respectively. Task-level cases show that restrictions on a shared capability can obstruct both legitimate and malicious operations, and that allowed tools or commands can leave unauthorized operations reachable through alternative execution paths. Harness providers should make security settings verifiable, test alternative execution paths to protected operations, and assess attack effects alongside task utility and execution costs.

Software Engineering.title: Reels-RSI: Program-Level Self-Improvement for Code-Rendered Explainer Videos
Software Engineering.summary: Explainer videos -- a worked geometry problem, why the sky is blue, how a dynasty fell -- are usually one more target for pixel video generation. We argue they are a different kind of artifact: a program (script, storyboard and per-frame animation code) that a deterministic renderer turns into frames. A program can be read, diffed, tested and audited; pixels can only be watched. Reels-RSI is an open-source reel director for any agent harness; its self-improvement happens at the program level rather than in weights or prompts. Every revision pass is logged with a code snapshot; a retrospective pairs each check finding with the diff that fixed it and proposes lessons; a lesson that a static check can catch is compiled into a rule with a must-fail and a must-pass example, so the memory is unit-tested; and a rule learned today runs over everything made before it. A bounded, benchmark-gated step lets an agent rewrite the director's playbook, kept only when blind pairwise judgments on held-out topics prefer it; nothing enters memory without a human decision. Across 111 reels -- a field study, two playbook evolutions, a 2x2 memory ablation, a weaker director, a 48-reel learning curve and a judge-reliability study -- we find that the rule learned in the field caught four latent defects in frames authored before it existed and none after; that rules are an audit for a strong director (eight unguarded reels, no violation) and a guard for a weaker one (thirty violations unguarded versus five); that lessons shorten revision loops but do not compound or move the judge; and that the first rewrite's 11--1 verdict was a position bias in our vote design (judges pick the second-shown reel 62--81% of the time), masking scripts that traded thirteen facts for craft. We document four failure modes of the preference signal, which check caught each, and the fixes. Code, rules, lessons and data are public.
Software Engineering.comment: 19 pages, 4 figures, 9 tables. Code, rules, lessons, data and evolve reports: https://github.com/agentic-loops-x/Reels-RSI

Software Engineering.title: What Counts as the Same Task? Executable Contracts for Robustness Evaluation of Tool-Using Agents
Software Engineering.summary: Robustness tests for tool-using agents often change the agent's environment, for example by hiding a hostile note in an invoice, and then judge the agent by what it does. The result tells us about the original task only if the changed test case is still a valid test of that task. Many evaluations decide this with weak rules, such as accepting any well-formed edit or any edit that stays close to the original in embedding space. We propose executable task contracts. A contract states which facts define a task, which edits are allowed, and what finishing the task means, and it checks each changed test case before the agent runs. We compare validity rules by scoring the same 14,336 stored agent runs under each rule. Across four encoders, embedding thresholds allowed 75-100% of edits that changed the task, such as swapping the payee, yet rejected 24-45% of valid hostile notes. With a MiniLM cosine threshold, Mistral appeared vulnerable on all 64 tasks, but only 26 had a successful valid attack. Replaying a saved solution and allowing edits to benchmark fields fail in similar ways. Evaluations should state, and check, what counts as the same task.

Software Engineering.title: When Is a Reconciliation Break Real? A Temporal Correctness Contract for Streaming Financial Reconciliation
Software Engineering.summary: Reconciliation systems decide, continuously, whether money the ledger expected has arrived at the bank. On an asynchronous stream that decision is taken against partial evidence: a credit that has not appeared may be missing, or may simply not have been posted yet. Deployed pipelines settle this with a timeout or a watermark, and the exceptions are treated as findings. We give a temporal correctness contract that says when such a verdict is admissible, relative to a declared per-source lateness bound, and a checker for it that needs no ground truth. The contract separates three things an operator otherwise sees only as a rising break rate: the reconciler decided too early, an input broke the bound it declared, or the money really is gone. On workloads from a published payment simulator, the standard remedy for a stalled streaming join, an idleness timeout, introduces contract violations on 5.42% of obligations (95% CI [3.94, 6.92]) on traffic where the same job without it is exactly sound, and violations vanish once the timeout reaches the slow source's posting period, as predicted. Under a lateness shift, all four identity-based reconcilers we test raise spurious breaks on between 18.3% and 23.0% of the credits the bank did settle, while their contract violation rate stays at or below 1.01%: the checker attributes the loss to 240 bank-side and 413 ledger-side bound violations rather than to the reconcilers. Tracking one horizon per source leaves break latency 12.7% lower on average and halves its tail (p99 224 against 446 ticks) at equal soundness, though it is not cheaper at every cost setting and we report where it loses. An Apache Flink interval join, written the ordinary way, violates the contract on 14.9--20.1% of obligations. The contract is expressible as SQL over the tables a reconciliation system already keeps, agreeing with the reference implementation on all 4,395 verdicts.
Software Engineering.comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables, 2 propositions. Code and reproducibility materials: https://github.com/abhisheksharma2411/reconstream (v1.0.2). Software archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23272623

Software Engineering.title: Rethinking SZZ Search Strategies: Lessons from Claude Code
Software Engineering.summary: Identifying bug-inducing commits (BICs) is important for studying software bugs and maintaining software, yet the accuracy of existing SZZ methods remains limited. Although various improvements have been proposed, many SZZ methods still rely on code tracing, which searches for BICs by tracing code changed in a bug-fixing commit (BFC) back to earlier commits. However, this approach may miss the actual BIC when the code responsible for introducing a bug differs from the code modified to fix it. To overcome this limitation, we investigate whether BIC identification can be improved by exploring search strategies that are not constrained to start with code tracing. We use Claude Code, a coding agent that has demonstrated high BIC identification accuracy in prior research, to explore such strategies. Rather than prescribing a search process or providing predefined candidate commits, we allow Claude Code to independently investigate a Git repository. We evaluate its identification accuracy and search behavior on 79 Java cases from 70 repositories. In 79.7% of runs, Claude Code reviewed commit histories before inspecting individual code diffs. It used commit messages to select changes for closer inspection. With this approach, Claude Code achieves an F1 score of 0.771, significantly outperforming all ten evaluated SZZ baselines. Our failure analysis also reveals incorrect oracle labels and ambiguities in BIC definitions in the studied evaluation dataset. After reconstructing the evaluation dataset to address these issues, Claude Code achieves an F1 score of 0.938. A key lesson from Claude Code for improving SZZ search strategies is to use semantic information to find relevant commits and then examine their code changes, rather than starting with code tracing.

Software Engineering.title: Re-executing Coding-Agent Evaluations: Unchanged Decisions and Unresolved Policy Risk
Software Engineering.summary: Executable tests grade large language model (LLM) coding-agent patches for leaderboards, rewards and self-improvement. Two preregistered re-execution studies returned negative results. SWE-bench Pro v1's offline option rejected none of 59 accepted Go patches whose grading configuration changed. Their exploratory, unweighted upper confidence limit is 4.95% under candidate independence, leaving a 3% exposed-patch risk unresolved; the preregistered estimator uses inverse sampling-probability weights. An extension was inconclusive. In a selected stratum, a reconstructed module cache built from the reference solution's dependencies rejected accepted alternatives from four models that passed with their own dependencies. Re-executing 1,929 selected agent-version/task evaluations from the Darwin Gödel Machine's archive preserved best-agent selection and system-variant ranking, with search history and scores of evaluations not rerun fixed. Exploratory host, image and adapted-grader comparisons also preserved them. Seven of 23 disagreements with archived verdicts did not recur on a second host; rebuilt images changed 16 three-run majority verdicts (0.83%) under four-CPU execution. We provide an evidence-to-claim summary, lessons for grader audits and an anonymous replication package. These results concern accepted patches and fixed-history decisions; general policy safety and adaptive-learning robustness require broader evaluations.

Software Engineering.title: SecReason: Vulnerability Detection and In-Stream Self-Repair for LLM Code Generation
Software Engineering.summary: Large language models (LLMs) may introduce security vulnerabilities into generated code, which can persist into production when verification focuses on functional correctness. Existing defenses act before, during, or after generation, but none inspects the code during generation. Security prompts and retrieved security knowledge act before any code exists, constrained decoding limits token choices but cannot guide repair, and post-hoc repair must regenerate the full response. Reasoning LLMs draft code early in their streamed chain of thought, and in this pre-delivery window the code exists only inside the reasoning stream. We present SecReason, an in-stream defense that monitors this window. Dual-track incremental scanning applies security rules, checking each statement as it is emitted and tracing dataflows across the accumulated code. When a security rule fires, SecReason interrupts generation, inserts an in-stream warning, and resumes decoding, so the model repairs the draft within the same reasoning trace without regenerating the full response. On tasks where unassisted generation introduces vulnerabilities, \system raises the share of runs delivering secure and functionally correct code from below 15\% to 72.8\%--98.1\% on \tool{CWEval} and \tool{SecCodeBench}. \system consumes fewer tokens than post-hoc repair, and when security rules misfire on secure code, it limits the functional regressions from false warnings.

Software Engineering.title: Kaizen: Metamorphic Fuzzing and Differential Testing for LLM-Translated HPC Applications
Software Engineering.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to port scientific codes across heterogeneous high-performance computing (HPC) programming models, such as translating CUDA to OpenMP, OpenACC, Kokkos or SYCL. However, current evaluations use compilation success, token-level similarity, or developer-written tests from static benchmarks, which cannot reliably ensure behavioral correctness. We present Kaizen, a metamorphic fuzzing and differential testing framework for evaluating the correctness of LLM-translated HPC code. Kaizen uses metamorphic fuzzing via source-code mutation to generate semantically equivalent programs, grammar-based input fuzzing to explore behavioral diversity, and differential testing to expose semantic divergences between original and translated applications that compile and pass developer-written tests yet produce incorrect scientific results. We evaluate Kaizen on CUDA-to-OpenMP translation of 16 scientific applications from seven domains using three fine-tuned LLMs at kernel-level and full-program granularity. Our evaluation reveals that (1) compilation success is a poor proxy for correctness; (2) LLM-translated programs exhibit systematic compile-time error patterns, with nine categories for kernel-level translation and 27 for full-program translation; (3) semantic errors that survive compilation are often input-dependent and require differential testing to expose; and (4) full-program translation is substantially harder than kernel-level translation. These findings highlight the need for correctness-oriented evaluation of LLM-assisted HPC code translations.

Software Engineering.title: Taylor-Approximation-Based Repair of High Floating-Point Errors
Software Engineering.summary:
Numerical libraries can still lose many bits of accuracy on localized ill-conditioned inputs, such as roots, poles, cancellation points, and branch boundaries. This paper presents NPTaylor, a Taylor-approximation-based framework for repairing localized high floating-point errors in numerical C routines. Given a high-error input, a localized repair domain, a high-precision oracle, and an error threshold, NPTaylor searches over Taylor degree, expansion center, segmentation, and floating-point evaluation strategy. It emits guarded C patches that use a generated Taylor evaluator inside the repair domain and fall back to the original routine outside it. Candidate patches are accepted only after validating the emitted C code on recorded local samples, guard endpoints, and the pre-repair peak input. The generated evaluator uses coefficient splitting and compensated Horner evaluation to reduce rounding error introduced by the patch itself.
  We evaluate NPTaylor on GSL benchmark workloads. On 38 one-input functions, both NPTaylor and AutoRNP repair all 114 configurations across three accuracy thresholds. NPTaylor is 3.33x faster by geometric-mean offline repair time and emits 0.162x as many C bytes. In the strictest setting, its median repair time is 3.74s versus 81.97s for AutoRNP. NPTaylor also repairs localized multi-input benchmark cases beyond AutoRNP's implemented one-input workflow. These results show that Taylor-based guarded patches can provide compact, efficient local repairs, while the claims remain validation-relative rather than full-domain proofs.

Software Engineering.title: Specification-Based Testing of Large Language Models
Software Engineering.summary: Model cards, system cards, and safety reports increasingly document LLM safety behaviors, yet safety evaluations typically start from predefined benchmarks rather than asking which documented claims those benchmarks actually test. We introduce LEST (LLM Evaluation through Specification-driven Testing), a framework that treats documented safety claims as specifications for black-box testing. In LEST, each claim determines which benchmark prompt tests it and whether a Refuse-to-Comply transition, where a model refuses a prompt but complies with its mutated version, counts as evidence against it. LEST mutates these prompts to search for counterexamples, manually validates each candidate, and traces validated counterexamples back to the claims they contradict. We evaluate LEST using the system cards of Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 with 97 seed prompts from SORRY-Bench across Mental Health and Self-Harm, Harmful and Violent Content, and Fairness and Bias. Of 56 identified safety claims, 29 (51.8%) are prompt-testable, but only 17 (58.6%) are exercised by an applicable benchmark prompt. Both models refuse >95% of benchmark prompts. Evaluating 1,836 mutated prompts on both models reveals 312 candidate Refuse-to-Comply transitions flagged by automated response classifiers. However, human validation confirms only 19 (6.1%) as both intent-preserving and genuinely compliant, showing automated evaluation substantially overestimates behavioral failures. Tracing these 19 transitions back to the claims reveals counterexamples for 6 of 9 covered claims for which refusal is an applicable oracle. Our results show that benchmark prompts may not be sufficient to validate all documented LLM safety behavior, and automated failure detection requires manual validation. LEST provides end-to-end traceability from natural-language safety documentation to executable tests and human-validated counterexamples.

Software Engineering.title: HoldSpec: A Machine-Checked Model and Conformance Suite for the Payment Authorization Hold Lifecycle
Software Engineering.summary: When a merchant authorizes a card and captures the funds later, the money sits in a state that neither party fully controls: held on the cardholder's account, not yet taken, and due to lapse on a deadline set by the card network. What a merchant may do to that hold, capture part of it, capture again, void it, raise it, let it expire, is business logic that every payment service provider implements slightly differently and none of them specifies formally. We give the lifecycle a state machine in TLA+, parameterized by a provider capability profile, and check eight safety invariants and three liveness properties over 6 profiles, five of them built from Stripe's and Adyen's published documentation. From the same machine we generate a conformance suite that runs black-box against a provider API. Against 61 seeded defects that are distinguishishable from a correct implementation, the generated suite detects 100%, where random sequences with the same call budget reach 56% and a hand-written integration suite reaches 69%; random sequences given ten times the budget still reach only 67%. Running the same suite between two providers turns the comparison into a search, and it returns short executable witnesses for divergences the two documentation sets imply but neither states, including one that breaks the common assumption that a single adapter interface can sit over both, because closing a hold and releasing its remainder is a capture on one provider and a cancel on the other. We report what we could not do: no provider sandbox credentials were available, so every result here concerns documented behavior, and the suite that would test the providers themselves is part of what we release.
Software Engineering.comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Code, TLA+ specification, generated conformance suite, mock providers, and reproducibility materials: https://github.com/abhisheksharma2411/holdspec. Software archived at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22244465

Performance.title: Delta Tokenizer: Reference-Identical Tokenization of Session Deltas and Segment-Parallelism for Long Prompts on Multicore CPUs
Performance.summary:
An agent that drives an LLM sends the model the same conversation again and again, and each turn adds only a little text at the end. Inference engines reuse the KV cache of the shared prefix, so only the new tokens pass through the model. However, tokenization has no such shortcut. The CPU front end of the serving engine converts every request back into token IDs from its first character, which lengthens the time to first token (TTFT) and consumes CPU on every turn.
  We present Delta Tokenizer, a CPU tokenization front end that tokenizes only the delta between a request and the previous request of the same session. It retains the earlier token sequence, encodes again only the appended text and the short tail whose tokens the append could affect, and joins the two only at a position the tokenizer's splitting rules themselves cannot move, which keeps the result exact. For long requests with no state to reuse, it cuts the text where practical tokenizers already keep neighboring pieces independent, encodes the pieces on several cores at once, and concatenates the outputs into the reference encoding, exactly. A shared CPU pool schedules these chunks together with the short incremental updates, so an update runs between two chunks rather than behind an entire long job.
  The incremental path shortens the tokenization of a session turn by roughly 40x relative to the Hugging Face reference tokenizer, and on 16 cores the chunk-parallel path encodes a four-million-character request 8.2x faster than a serial encode and 1.6-2.1x faster than LoPT. Inside SGLang, Delta Tokenizer reduces the median TTFT through the chat interface by 59% at 100K tokens and brings the P99 TTFT of agent sessions down 9.5x under load and 23x when long requests tie up the front end. Every output we checked matches the reference, among them 41.8 billion documents encoded by its fast encoder.
Performance.comment: 42 pages (16-page main text, references, and supplementary material), 14 figures, 35 tables. The incremental tokenization path and the fast encoder are open source in toktier at https://github.com/asu-idi/toktier. The chunk-parallel path, the CPU pool scheduler, and the SGLang adapter will be released in the same repository

Performance.title: How the Dirty Set Moves: Characterizing Schedule Reuse in Incremental Sparse Matrix Multiplication
Performance.summary: Sparse matrices, in which most entries are zero, are central to scientific simulation, graph analytics and machine learning, and their multiplication with dense inputs is a core parallel kernel. In many applications the matrix stays fixed while only a few input rows change per step, so the result can be updated from those rows alone, which we call the dirty set. Sparse kernels often add a second optimization based on the inspector-executor principle, in which a tiled schedule is prepared once and reused across calls. However, when this reuse remains profitable as the dirty set moves is not well characterized. In this paper, we show that retained tiled execution rarely beats direct CSC in incremental sparse matrix multiplication, although incremental execution itself remains highly profitable. Across 21 SuiteSparse matrices and controlled patterns of motion, a direct column-wise incremental update is 2.1-8.2x faster than the best of eight full-recomputation codes, among them Intel oneMKL and PyTorch. Yet the same direct update outperforms a tiled executor that retains tile preparation and caches assembled schedules in 779 of 837 workloads. Separating reuse into per-tile preparation and cached schedules shows that the benefit comes from preparation; extra cache capacity seldom helps because a tile set rarely returns after a different one has intervened. Tiling is faster only when tiles merge many entries into each output write, a structural property that we predicted before measurement and confirmed on four held-out matrices of the same family. These results show that the structure of the matrix and the motion of the dirty set, rather than the sophistication of the schedule, determine whether reuse is profitable. We anticipate that our methodology and guidelines will help developers decide when to build schedule reuse into incremental sparse runtimes.
Performance.comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, 8 tables

Performance.title: Scaling LLM Inference via Parallelism: Throughput-Latency Trade-off
Performance.summary: Large Language Model (LLM) serving systems must balance latency and throughput while efficiently utilizing distributed GPU resources. This challenge arises because inference consists of two fundamentally different phases: prefill, which determines time-to-first-token (TTFT), and decode, which determines inter-token latency (ITL). The use of tensor parallelism (TP), pipeline parallelism (PP), and hybrid configurations exposes different trade-offs between these latency dimensions, making the optimal parallelism configuration highly dependent on workload characteristics, latency requirements, and context length. Moreover, despite the widespread adoption of distributed inference, there is still limited understanding of how parallelism configurations should be selected under varying workload conditions and service-level objectives (SLO). In this paper, we develop a systematic framework for characterizing LLM inference parallelism via throughput-latency trade-offs, SLO-aware serving, and long-context scalability. We introduce the notion of parallelism operating regions by constructing TTFT-ITL feasible sets and Pareto frontiers across different workload compositions, thereby revealing a systematic transition from TP-dominant to PP-dominant configurations as workloads become increasingly prefill-heavy. We further formulate SLO-aware parallelism selection using goodput, showing that stringent TTFT requirements favor PP-dominated configurations, whereas relaxed latency constraints progressively shift the optimality toward TP-dominated configurations with higher serving capacity. Finally, we demonstrate that increasing context length fundamentally changes the relative advantages of parallelism configurations, with PP-dominant configurations exhibiting more favorable scalability and SLO attainment in the long-context regime.
Performance.comment: 15 pages, 7 figures

Hardware Architecture.title: STISA: A 0.16 GOPS/W/PE Single-Shot Inference FPGA-based SNN Accelerator with Algorithm and Hardware Co-Design
Hardware Architecture.summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer great potential for low-power intelligent computing owing to their event-driven nature, yet their deployment is limited by high inference latency and inefficient hardware utilization caused by temporal dependencies. Existing accelerators struggle to balance timesteps, accuracy, and energy efficiency, while hardware-oriented timestep compression remains underexplored. To address these challenges, this work presents STISA, a unified algorithm-hardware co-design framework featuring: (i) a Temporal Splitter Compression (TSC) technique with a Temporal Split Structure (TSS) to reduce temporal redundancy while preserving network dynamics; (ii) a hardware-efficient spatiotemporal parallelism scheme, which co-optimizes dataflow and architecture through a Temporal-Prioritized Output-Stationary (TPOS) mapping and a flexible Block-Mux Streaming (BMS) architecture; and (iii) a joint TSC-TPOS-BMS co-optimization framework featuring a bandwidth-aware resource allocation strategy to achieve balanced accuracy, latency, and energy efficiency across diverse network architectures. On the algorithmic side, TSC reduces synaptic operations by 24.44%-51.71% while achieving competitive accuracies of 96.38%, 81.10%, 68.51%, and 82.40% on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and DVS-CIFAR10, respectively. On the hardware side, FPGA prototypes deliver up to 7.99 speedup, 30.4% power reduction, and 30.1% LUT reduction. Compared with state-of-the-art SNN accelerators, STISA achieves 0.16 GOPS/W/PE, demonstrating its scalability and superior energy efficiency for real-time SNN inference under constrained hardware resources.
Hardware Architecture.comment: Author accepted manuscript. Published in IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems I: Regular Papers

Hardware Architecture.title: CAFE: Conducting-Cell-Aware Adaptive Differential Encoding for Robust DNN Inference in FeFET-Based Compute-in-Memory
Hardware Architecture.summary: Ferroelectric field-effect transistor (FeFET)-based compute-in-memory (CIM) promises energy-efficient deep neural network (DNN) inference, but device variation can severely degrade bit-sliced CIM accuracy. Prior works either rely on hardware modifications or treat such variation as generic noise, overlooking a key FeFET asymmetry: negligible off-state leakage makes errors dominated by conducting on-state cells. This asymmetry is amplified by two's-complement sign extension, which maps small negative values to high-significance bit slices and magnifies their errors during shift-and-add reconstruction. In this paper, we propose CAFE, a conducting-cell-aware adaptive differential encoding framework built upon this FeFET-specific asymmetry. CAFE introduces C$^2$AM, a bit-significance-weighted conducting-cell activity metric that predicts output deviation and inference accuracy degradation under FeFET device variation. Guided by C$^2$AM, CAFE applies differential weight and activation encoding to eliminate sign-extension-induced conducting-cell amplification. To balance robustness and cost, CAFE performs type-wise encoding enumeration, layer-wise NSGA-II search, and post-GA pruning to allocate robust encodings where the robustness-cost trade-off is favorable. Across representative vision and language workloads, CAFE reduces C$^2$AM by up to $28.6\times$; in the main deployment study, it improves accuracy over two's-complement CIM by more than 87 percentage points and approaches full-differential robustness at $1.86$-$2.78\times$ normalized cost, compared with $3.06\times$ for uniform full-differential encoding.
Hardware Architecture.comment: Full version of the paper accepted to the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Computer Design (ICCD). 16 figures, 1 table

Hardware Architecture.title: ESL-former: Event Sparse Linear Transformer for FPGA-Accelerated Malware Detection
Hardware Architecture.summary: Transformer based intrusion detection has shown strong potential for identifying unknown malware variants, but its deployment on resource constrained edge devices remains difficult due to the high computational and memory cost of self attention. This paper presents an event sparse Linear Transformer framework for malware detection on FPGA edge platforms. Instead of relying on an explicit attention matrix, the proposed method derives token and channel importance directly from the accumulated key value state of Linear Transformer. A contribution aware scoring function is introduced to measure the perturbation of each token or kernel channel to the linear attention state, allowing redundant tokens and low contribution channels to be removed without constructing quadratic attention maps. To translate sparsity into practical hardware acceleration, the proposed design further replaces conventional binary mask based execution with a Top K active token buffer and a hardware compaction unit. The selected active tokens and channels are reorganized into dense fixed length data streams, enabling downstream processing elements to execute regular multiply accumulate operations with reduced redundant memory access and control overhead. This design is suitable for low power FPGA based malware detection, where both latency and on chip resource usage are critical. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that the proposed sparse Linear Transformer can reduce hardware cost while preserving malware classification accuracy.
Hardware Architecture.comment: Accepted at ICA3PP 2026. 19 pages, 5 figures

Hardware Architecture.title: MFSA: A Multi-Format Systolic Array with Native Micro Scaling Support
Hardware Architecture.summary: AI workloads increasingly employ low-precision formats such as BF16 / FP16, FP8 variants, FP4, Micro Scaling (MX), and INT modes across models, layers, and execution stages to balance accuracy, memory footprint, and throughput, which in turn requires hardware to support these formats in a flexible and efficient way. We present MFSA, a weight-stationary multi-format systolic array that achieves area efficiency through two architectural choices. At the PE level, MFSA uses dot-product-accumulator-based processing elements extended from an existing open-source trans-precision FPU to support reduced-precision formats (FP32/FP16/BF16/CFP8/FP4/INT16/INT8/INT4) with a shared datapath and proportional throughput scaling. At the array level, MFSA employs Online Block-Scale Rebasing (OBSR) for block-scaled formats, which folds each block scale into the running FP32 partial sum at block boundaries without adding a second cross-block accumulator, thereby reducing the additional overhead of block-scaling support. In TSMC 28 nm at 1 GHz, matched-throughput BF16/FP8/FP4 cascaded FMA-PE baselines are 1.5x/2.5x/4.5x larger than the single-format DPA-PE, the gap growing with subword parallelism. A routed 16x16 MFSA reaches a peak 0.5/1/2/4 TOPS of FP32/BF16/FP8/FP4, and OBSR cuts the incremental MX overhead by 64.2% in area and 67.5% in energy versus a naive MX implementation baseline, without hurting the numerical stability on real LLM traces. Adding support for all other formats based on a BF16+CFP8 systolic array costs 25.7% additional area. OBSR also extends to non-power-of-two block scales: folding the fractional part of an E4M3 scale into the MFPE dot product supports NVFP4 alongside OCP MX for 11.8% area and 7.3% power over a CFP8+FP4 base, less than half the cost of a naive implementation.
Hardware Architecture.comment: Accepted to the 44th IEEE International Conference on Computer Design (ICCD 2026)

Hardware Architecture.title: PAGE404: Breaking GPU Isolation Through Hardware-assisted Page Migration
Hardware Architecture.summary: NVIDIA's Grace Hopper (GH200) superchip represents a new generation of heterogeneous computing, tightly integrating a 72-core Arm-based CPU with a Hopper GPU on a single module via a high-bandwidth, cache-coherent interconnect. By eliminating the conventional PCIe bottleneck for CPU-GPU data movement, this design establishes a unified memory domain that scales to the capacities demanded by generative AI and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads. The architecture also introduces hardware-assisted page migration: driven by access counters, the system dynamically promotes frequently accessed pages from host CPU memory to GPU DRAM to improve memory locality. We study the security of this emerging architecture against new side- and covert-channel attacks targeting its page migration support. We analyze counter-driven migration across both the hardware mechanisms and the UVM driver's interrupt-handling pipeline, and identify two side-channel vulnerabilities: one rooted in the shared structure of access counters, and the other in the driver's response to migration interrupts. We further show that both channels are exploitable across Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions, a feature intended to provide strong, hardware-enforced isolation between co-located tenants. Using proof-of-concept attacks, we build covert channels that reach roughly 8,500 bits per second through eviction-based signaling and 8,100 bits per second through migration-delay-based signaling across MIG instances. The interrupt-based channel also fingerprints inference workloads across distinct large language models (LLMs) and CPU SPEC2017 benchmarks, and estimates the prompt length processed during LLM inference with high accuracy. These results expose a security gap in hardware-managed heterogeneous memory systems and call into question the isolation guarantees of current MIG-enabled multi-tenant GPU deployments.

Hardware Architecture.title: Foundations of Hardware-Software Leakage Contracts
Hardware Architecture.summary:
Microarchitectural attacks such as Spectre and Meltdown undermine security by exploiting software-visible side effects of microarchitectural optimizations like caches and speculative execution. To use modern hardware securely, programmers must take into account the security implications of these optimizations. Yet instruction set architectures (ISAs)---the conventional abstraction layer between hardware and software---are ill-suited for secure programming: by design, they abstract from microarchitectural details and therefore fail to reflect their security consequences.
  A new security abstraction is emerging to fill this void: hardware-software leakage contracts. To support the principled development of secure software on modern hardware such contracts characterize side-channel leakage at the ISA level. Thereby they enable programmers and compilers to generate code that is provably resistant to side-channel attacks---without having to explicitly reason about the microarchitecture. On the other hand, they provide a specification for hardware designers to ensure that microarchitectures do not introduce unintended and undocumented side channels. This paper introduces the foundations of this emerging topic, discussing recent contributions and unresolved challenges along the way.
Hardware Architecture.comment: Author's manuscript. Final publication is available at Springer via https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-95-8617-2_4

Hardware Architecture.title: Arcalís: Accelerating Remote Procedure Calls Using a Líghtweight Near-Cache Solution
Hardware Architecture.summary: Modern microservices increasingly depend on high-performance remote procedure calls (RPCs) to coordinate fine-grained, distributed computation. As network bandwidths continue to scale, the CPU overhead associated with RPC processing, particularly serialization, deserialization, and protocol handling, has become a critical bottleneck. This challenge is exacerbated by fast user-space networking stacks such as DPDK, which expose RPC processing as the dominant performance limiter. While prior hardware accelerators have explored NIC-attached and FPGA-based offload, these approaches remain farther from the cache hierarchy, so the frequent data accesses during RPC processing each pay an extra interconnect traversal cost that inflates RPC time. Therefore, RPC handling should occur as close as possible to the cache; however, a near-cache solution must be small, hence practical and deployable. Our key insight to enable such a solution is taking advantage of a reconfigurable accelerator that can be configured specifically for the services currently running on the CPUs. We present Arcalís, a near-cache RPC accelerator that positions a lightweight hardware engine adjacent to the last-level cache (LLC). Arcalís offloads RPC processing to dedicated microengines that operate with cache-line latency while preserving programmability. By decoupling RPC processing logic, enabling microservice-specific execution, and positioning itself near the LLC, Arcalís achieves a 1.72-4.91$\times$ end-to-end speedup compared to the CPU baseline, significantly reduces microarchitectural overhead by up to 88\%, and achieves up to a 1.67$\times$ higher throughput than prior solutions. These results highlight the potential of near-cache RPC acceleration as a practical solution for high-performance microservice deployment.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 14 pages, 26 figures

Hardware Architecture.title: A LoRa-Compatible Receiver with Programmable Noise-Power Trade-Off and Integrated Wake-Up Mode
Hardware Architecture.summary: Programmable receivers allow an optimal performance in the variable conditions of the wireless channel. An extensive analysis of their noise-power trade-off enables the development of a main receiver with embedded wake-up circuitry. This makes the seamless integration of wake-up receivers (WuRXs) in RF receivers possible, avoiding power, area, complexity, and cost overheads in the system. In this paper, we propose the first LoRa-compatible receiver with an integrated wake-up mode and a programmable noise-power trade-off. In main-receiver mode, it consumes 4.57 mW for a sensitivity of -138 dBm, but it can save up to 62.6% of power consumption at the cost of an 8.3-dB sensitivity degradation. In wake-up mode, sensitivity down to -126 dBm is achieved for a 32-ms latency and 1.5 mW of power consumption. The power consumption remains relatively high due to a sub-optimal design of the the phase-locked loop (PLL). In the end, the wake-up mode consumes 3X less than the lowest-noise configuration in main-receiver mode.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 13 pages, 19 figures, submitted to TCAS-I journal

Cryptography and Security.title: AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities
Cryptography and Security.summary: Capability evaluations aim to surface dangerous model behaviors before deployment, but their reliability depends on the assumption that hidden capabilities can be elicited.
